title: Careers and Pathways in Digital Technology
summary: Where digital skills can take you: the main tech career areas and what people do day to day, the Northern Ireland tech sector, GCSE, A level, university and apprenticeship routes, and how to build a portfolio, CV and careers plan.
learn: Why digital skills matter in almost every job
Six tech career areas, what each person does day to day, and how KS3 topics such as user-centred design, accessibility, AI, encryption and sustainability lead into them
The Northern Ireland tech sector, types of employer and hybrid working
Routes: GCSE (CCEA Route B Programming), A level, university and apprenticeships in NI
The skills employers want and how to prove them with STAR, a portfolio and a skills-based CV
Your online reputation, diversity in tech, and writing your own SMART careers plan
intro: You are about to choose your GCSEs, so it is a good time to ask where Digital Technology can lead. This topic explores tech careers and what people really do all day, the tech industry here in Northern Ireland, the qualification routes from GCSE to apprenticeships and university, and how to start building your skills, portfolio and careers plan now.

pages.spec: Explain why digital skills are needed in almost every job, not only in 'computer jobs'
pages.summary: Nearly every job now uses digital technology, from farming and nursing to retail and sport. Digital skills, plus transferable skills such as problem solving, make you more employable whatever career you choose.

diagram.title: Digital tech in jobs you might not expect
diagram.caption: Match each job to one way it uses digital technology.
pairs: Sensors and apps track milk yield and animal health
Updates electronic patient records on a tablet
Sells online and checks stock in a spreadsheet
Analyses match video and GPS data on players
Plugs in a diagnostic computer to find engine faults
Records, edits and releases songs with digital software

blocks.text: When you hear the words *tech job*, you might picture someone in a hoodie typing green code on a black screen. Some tech jobs do involve lots of coding, but that picture leaves out almost everyone. Today, **nearly every job uses digital technology** in some way.

**[[Digital skills]]** are the abilities you need to use, understand and create with digital technology: from sending a professional email or using a spreadsheet, to keeping data secure, to writing code.
Digital technology is everywhere

head: Sector
How it uses digital technology
rows: GPS-guided tractors, milking robots, apps that record each animal's health and feed.
Electronic patient records, scanners that produce digital images, online appointment booking.
Online shops, card payments, stock control systems, data about what customers buy.
Video analysis, wearable GPS trackers, fitness data, ticketing apps.
Computer-controlled machines, 3D design software, robots on the production line.
Digital music, animation, film editing, social media marketing.
blocks.caption: Digital technology across different sectors

blocks.text: This means that even if you never want to be a programmer, the skills you build in Digital Technology will help you in whatever job you choose.
Why do employers care so much?

items: **Technology keeps changing.** People who are confident learning new software adapt quickly when their workplace changes.
**[[Automation]]** means computers now do many repetitive tasks, such as scanning barcodes or sorting emails. People are needed to set up, check and improve these systems.
**Data is valuable.** Businesses want people who can collect, organise and make sense of data.
**Security matters.** One careless click on a phishing email can cost a business a lot, so every worker needs basic cyber security habits.

blocks.text: Transferable skills

A **[[Transferable skill]]** is a skill you can take from one job or subject to another. Digital Technology is full of them: breaking a big problem into smaller parts, testing your work, explaining your ideas to others and not giving up when your code will not run.

blocks.title: Worked example: spot the digital skills
blocks.context: Orla works in a café in Enniskillen. List three digital skills she might use in a normal day.
steps: She takes card and phone payments on a till system: **using digital devices confidently**.
She updates the café's social media with a photo of the soup of the day: **creating digital content for an audience**.
She enters the week's sales into a spreadsheet so the owner can see which cakes sell best: **handling data**.
blocks.answer: Even a job that does not sound like a tech job uses several digital skills every day.

blocks.text: Do not think 'I'm not going to work in IT, so this doesn't matter.' Most employers now list digital skills as essential, whatever the job title.
In Northern Ireland your school has access to careers advisers from the **Careers Service** (part of the Department for the Economy). They can help you see how the subjects you choose link to jobs.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Nearly every job now uses digital technology.
Digital skills range from using software confidently to writing code.
Automation means people are needed to set up, check and improve computer systems.
Transferable skills such as problem solving move with you from job to job.
Digital Technology helps your career even if you do not become a programmer.

check.q: Which statement about digital skills is most accurate?
o: They are only needed by programmers
They are useful in almost every job
They are only needed in offices
They are no longer needed because of AI
check.why: Farming, health, retail, sport and many more all use digital technology.

check.q: What is a transferable skill?
o: A skill that can be used in many different jobs or subjects
A skill you can only use in one job
A skill that is copied from a website
check.why: Transferable skills, such as problem solving, move with you from one job to another.

check.q: A farmer uses an app that records each cow's health. This is an example of...
o: A job with no digital skills
Digital technology in a non-computing job
check.why: Farming is not a 'computer job', but it uses digital technology every day.

check.q: Why do employers want staff with basic cyber security habits?
o: So staff can avoid writing reports
One careless click on a phishing email could harm the whole business
check.why: Every worker who uses email or the internet can let an attacker in.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **digital skills**.
practice.a: The abilities needed to use, understand (1) and create with digital technology, e.g. using spreadsheets, emailing professionally, coding (1).

practice.q: Choose a job that does not sound like a 'tech job'. Describe **two** ways a person in that job uses digital technology.
practice.a: Any suitable job (e.g. nurse) with two sensible uses (1 each), e.g. electronic patient records; booking systems.

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why employers value staff with good digital skills.
practice.a: Any two: technology keeps changing so they adapt quickly (1); automation needs people to set up/check systems (1); data is valuable (1); cyber security (1).

pages.spec: Describe what software developers, cyber security analysts and data scientists do day to day
pages.summary: Software developers plan, write, test and improve programs in cycles. Cyber security analysts protect systems from attack. Data scientists and AI specialists find patterns in data and build models that make predictions.

diagram.title: How a software team builds an app
diagram.caption: Software development is a cycle: the team keeps planning, building, testing and refining.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Talk to users and write user stories such as 'As a pupil, I want to see my homework on my phone so that I don't forget it.'

items.label: Design
items.detail: Sketch screens and plan how the data and code will be organised.

items.label: Develop
items.detail: Write the code in a text-based language such as Python, C# or JavaScript.

items.label: Test
items.detail: Try normal, boundary and wrong data to find bugs before users do.

items.label: Release and refine
items.detail: Users try it, give feedback, and the cycle starts again to improve it.

blocks.text: Tech is not one job: it is a whole family of careers. On this page and the next we look at **six main career areas** and what people in them actually do all day. First: software, cyber security, and data and AI.
1. Software development

A **[[Software developer]]** (also called a programmer or software engineer) designs, writes, tests and improves programs: apps, websites, games, the software in cars and medical machines, and the systems banks and shops run on.

items: Meets with the team each morning to agree what to work on (often called a *stand-up* meeting).
Reads **user stories**: short descriptions of what a user needs, e.g. *'As a customer, I want to track my parcel so that I know when to be in.'*
Writes and reviews code, often in pairs or small teams.
Tests code and fixes **bugs** (errors that make a program go wrong).
Uses generative AI tools to suggest code, but **checks and tests everything they produce**, because AI can be confidently wrong.

blocks.text: Software is built in **cycles** of planning, developing, testing and refining. That is exactly what you do when you write a program in class, test it and improve it.
2. Cyber security

A **[[Cyber security analyst]]** watches an organisation's systems for signs of attack and responds when something goes wrong. Other cyber jobs include penetration testers (ethical hackers who test systems with permission), digital forensics investigators and security engineers.

items: Checks alerts: a login from an unusual country at 3 am, or a computer suddenly sending lots of data.
Makes sure data is protected with **encryption**, for example HTTPS on websites.
Trains staff to spot phishing emails.
Writes reports explaining what happened and how to stop it happening again.

blocks.text: 3. Data science and artificial intelligence

A **[[Data scientist]]** collects and cleans large amounts of data, then looks for patterns that help people make decisions. Many also build **AI models**, which learn patterns from large datasets to make predictions or generate content.

items: Cleans messy data: removing duplicates and fixing mistakes.
Uses databases and code to pick out the data that answers a question.
Builds charts and dashboards so managers can see what the data shows.
Trains and tests AI models, and checks them for unfairness (bias).

blocks.title: Worked example: which career area?
blocks.context: Which career area does each task belong to? (a) Investigating why a hospital's network suddenly slowed down at night. (b) Predicting how many buses Translink will need on a Saturday using past passenger data. (c) Adding a 'dark mode' button to a school app after users asked for it.
steps: (a) Looking for signs of an attack on a network: **cyber security**.
(b) Finding patterns in past data to make a prediction: **data science and AI**.
(c) Changing a program to meet a user need: **software development**.
blocks.answer: Cyber security, then data science and AI, then software development.

blocks.text: A common myth is that tech people work alone all day. In real teams, developers, analysts and data scientists spend a lot of time talking, planning and explaining their work to others.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Software developers plan, write, test and refine programs in cycles.
User stories describe what users need from a program.
Cyber security analysts watch for and respond to attacks.
Data scientists find patterns in data and build AI models.
AI tools can suggest code, but people must check and test it.

check.q: Which job involves watching systems for signs of attack?
check.why: Cyber security analysts monitor systems and respond to attacks.

check.q: What is a user story?
o: A short description of what a user needs and why
A review of an app on an app store
A diary kept by a programmer
A list of bugs found in testing
check.why: e.g. 'As a pupil, I want... so that...' helps developers plan what to build.

check.q: A developer uses an AI tool to suggest some code. What should they do next?
o: Delete it because AI code is illegal
Ask the AI if it is correct
Read and test it carefully before using it
check.why: AI can produce code that looks right but contains errors, so people must review and test it.

check.q: Which task is most typical of a data scientist?
o: Finding patterns in sales data to predict demand
check.why: Data scientists analyse data to find patterns and make predictions.

practice.q: Describe **two** tasks a software developer might do in a normal working day.
practice.a: Any two: write code (1); test and fix bugs (1); attend team stand-up (1); read user stories / plan (1); review others' code (1).

practice.q: Write a user story for a school canteen app.
practice.a: Uses the format As a..., I want... (1) so that... with a sensible reason (1), e.g. As a pupil, I want to top up my account on my phone so that I don't need cash.

practice.q: Explain why a developer should test code produced by a generative AI tool.
practice.a: AI can produce code that looks correct but has errors/security problems (1); the developer is responsible, so testing makes sure it works properly (1).

pages.spec: Describe what network and cloud engineers, web, UX and games designers, and IT support technicians do, and link each career area to KS3 Digital Technology
pages.summary: Network and cloud engineers keep data moving and stored safely; web, UX and games designers create products around users' needs; IT support technicians keep everyone's technology working. Everything you learn at KS3 leads somewhere.

diagram.title: Meet the tech team
diagram.caption: A tech company in Belfast might have all of these people. Click each one to see what they do.

rows.label: Software developer
rows.detail: Writes, tests and refines the code for the company's app.

rows.label: UX designer
rows.detail: Interviews users and makes the app easy, accessible and pleasant to use.

rows.label: Games designer
rows.detail: Plans the rules, levels and story of a game, then tests that it is fun.

rows.label: Cyber security analyst
rows.detail: Watches for attacks and makes sure data is encrypted.

rows.label: Data scientist
rows.detail: Finds patterns in the app's data and trains AI models.

rows.label: Network and cloud engineer
rows.detail: Keeps the network and cloud servers running, fast and secure.

rows.label: IT support technician (help desk)
rows.detail: Sets up laptops, resets passwords and fixes problems for staff. A common first job in tech.

blocks.text: 4. Networking and cloud

A **[[Network engineer]]** designs, builds and looks after the networks that connect computers: cables, fibre, wireless access points, routers and switches. Many now also work with **[[Cloud computing]]**: storing data and running software on servers in data centres, reached over the internet, instead of on your own device.

items: Sets up and tests network equipment and wireless coverage.
Checks the network is fast, reliable and secure.
Manages cloud servers, deciding how much storage and processing power is needed.
Thinks about **sustainability**: data centres use a lot of electricity and water for cooling, so efficient designs matter.

blocks.text: 5. Web, UX and games design

A **[[UX designer]]** (UX means *user experience*) works out what users need and designs apps and websites that are easy to use. They use **user-centred design**: asking *who* a product is for, not just whether it works.

items: Interviews and observes real users, then writes user stories.
Sketches wireframes and builds clickable prototypes.
Tests designs with users and **refines** them to improve usability.
Checks **accessibility**: following guidelines such as **WCAG** so people with sight, hearing, movement or learning difficulties can use the product.

blocks.text: A **[[Games designer]]** plans the rules, levels, characters and story of a game, then tests and adjusts it until it is fun and fair. Web developers build the websites themselves using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
6. IT support

An **[[IT support technician]]** keeps everyone else's technology working: setting up laptops and accounts, resetting passwords, fixing printers and answering questions on the help desk. Your school's IT technicians do this job every day. It is a very common **first job** in tech, and many people move on from it into networking or cyber security.
Where does KS3 Digital Technology lead?

head: What you learn at KS3
Career area that uses it
How it is used at work
rows: Building and improving real apps in cycles
Designing products around real users' needs
Making sure everyone can use a website or app
Protecting data as it travels across networks
How AI learns patterns from data
Building fast, reliable school and business networks
Environmental cost of cloud and AI
Choosing energy-efficient data centres and designs
Testing ideas before building the real thing
blocks.caption: From the classroom to the workplace

blocks.title: Worked example: matching interests to careers
blocks.context: Three Year 10 pupils describe what they enjoy. Suggest a career area for each. (a) Ciara loves drawing and always notices when an app is confusing to use. (b) Darragh is the person his family asks to fix the Wi-Fi. (c) Ella enjoyed finding patterns in the spreadsheet topic and wants to know how AI works.
steps: (a) Design plus caring about users: **web, UX and games design**.
(b) Enjoys networks and fixing problems: **networking and cloud**, perhaps starting in **IT support**.
(c) Patterns in data and AI: **data science and AI**.
blocks.answer: UX design, networking (via IT support) and data science. These are starting points to explore, not fixed decisions.

blocks.text: Do not confuse UX with *looking nice*. A beautiful app that users cannot work out how to use, or that a screen reader cannot read, has **poor** user experience.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Network and cloud engineers keep data moving and stored securely.
UX designers use user-centred design, user stories and accessibility guidelines.
Games designers plan rules and levels, then test that the game is fun.
IT support is a common first job in tech.
Every KS3 topic links to at least one career area.

check.q: What does UX stand for?
check.why: UX designers focus on the user's experience of a product.

check.q: Which job is a common first job in tech, often leading to networking or cyber security?
check.why: IT support builds broad experience of systems and users.

check.q: A designer checks that a website works with a screen reader. What are they checking?
check.why: Accessibility guidelines such as WCAG help everyone use a product.

check.q: Why do cloud engineers think about sustainability?
o: Data centres use lots of electricity and water
Cloud data is printed on paper
check.why: Running and cooling data centres has a real environmental cost.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **user-centred design**.
practice.a: Designing a product around the needs of its users (1), e.g. by interviewing/testing with real users and refining the design (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** tasks an IT support technician might do.
practice.a: Any two: set up laptops/accounts (1); reset passwords (1); fix printers/hardware (1); answer help desk queries (1).

practice.q: Choose one KS3 Digital Technology topic you have studied. Explain how it links to a career.
practice.a: Names a topic (1) and links it sensibly to a job and how it is used (1), e.g. web design leads to web developer building accessible sites.

pages.spec: Describe the tech sector in Northern Ireland, the types of employer and how hybrid and remote working affect where you can work
pages.summary: Northern Ireland, especially Belfast, has a large software and cyber security industry. Tech jobs also exist in hospitals, councils, banks, manufacturers and small local firms, and hybrid or remote working means you do not always have to live in Belfast.

diagram.title: Test yourself: the NI tech sector
diagram.caption: Think of your answer, then click to check.
head: Question
Answer

About how many cyber security firms were in NI in 2023?
About how many people worked in NI cyber security in 2023?
Name a non-tech employer that hires tech staff
e.g. a hospital trust, council, bank or manufacturer
Splitting the week between the office and home
Which Belfast research centre focuses on cyber security?

blocks.text: You do not have to leave Northern Ireland to have a career in tech. The **[[Tech sector]]** (all the businesses whose main product is software, digital services or technology) is an important and growing part of the NI economy.
Belfast: software and cyber security

Belfast is known internationally for **software development** and especially **cyber security**. Many large international companies have offices there, alongside lots of local software firms and start-ups.

head: Fact (2023 snapshot)
Figure
rows: Cyber security firms in Northern Ireland
People working in NI cyber security
Share of those firms based in Belfast
blocks.caption: Northern Ireland Cybersecurity Snapshot 2023 (CSIT, Queen's University Belfast)

blocks.text: Part of the reason is education and research: **CSIT** (the Centre for Secure Information Technologies) at **Queen's University Belfast** is a major cyber security research centre, and NI's universities and colleges train thousands of computing students.
Figures like these change every year. Treat them as a snapshot, not a fixed fact, and check up-to-date careers information when you are making real choices.
Types of employer

head: Type of employer
Example of tech work there
rows: International tech and financial companies with Belfast offices
Software development, cyber security, data analysis
Building apps and websites for clients; small teams where you try lots of roles
The public sector (health trusts, councils, the civil service, the police)
Keeping vital systems running and patient or citizen data secure
Manufacturers and engineering firms, including in the west of NI
Computer-controlled machines, design software, factory networks
IT support, network management, teaching computing
Building websites or apps for local businesses
blocks.caption: Tech jobs are not only in tech companies

blocks.text: Where will you work? Office, hybrid or remote

Many tech jobs can be done anywhere with a good internet connection. **[[Hybrid working]]** means splitting your week between the office and home. **[[Remote working]]** means working from home (or anywhere) nearly all the time.

head: Hybrid or remote working
Working in the office every day
rows: Daily travel, e.g. Enniskillen to Belfast is a long drive
You could live in Fermanagh and work for a Belfast or even overseas company
You usually need to live near the office
Harder to pick up tips by sitting beside experienced staff
Easy to ask colleagues and learn by watching
Uses online collaboration tools, video calls and shared workspaces

blocks.title: Worked example: weighing up a job
blocks.context: Niall lives near Enniskillen. He is offered a software job with a Belfast company: two days a week in the office, three at home. Give one advantage and one disadvantage.
steps: Advantage: he only travels to Belfast twice a week, so he can stay living in Fermanagh and save travel time and money.
Disadvantage: on home days he cannot easily learn from experienced colleagues sitting beside him, and he needs a reliable internet connection.
blocks.answer: Hybrid working opens up Belfast jobs to people across NI, but it needs good self-organisation and online communication.

blocks.text: Do not assume every tech job is remote. Some roles, such as IT support and network engineering, need you on site to handle the actual equipment, and many employers want new starters in the office more often.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Belfast is a major centre for software and cyber security.
In 2023 there were about 124 cyber security firms in NI, most in Belfast.
Tech jobs exist in hospitals, councils, banks, manufacturers and small firms, not just tech companies.
Hybrid working splits the week between office and home; remote working is mostly from home.
Remote work widens choice but can make learning from colleagues harder.

check.q: Which NI city has most of the region's cyber security firms?
check.why: About 85% of NI cyber security firms were based in Belfast in 2023.

check.q: What is hybrid working?
o: Splitting the week between the office and home
check.why: Hybrid working mixes office days and home days.

check.q: Which of these employers is LEAST likely to be called a 'tech company' but still hires tech staff?
check.why: Hospitals need IT support, network engineers and security staff too.

check.q: Give a disadvantage of fully remote working for a new starter.
o: It is harder to learn by watching experienced colleagues
You must live next to the office
You have to commute every day
check.why: New starters often learn a lot by sitting beside experienced staff.

practice.q: Name **three** types of employer in Northern Ireland that employ people with digital skills.
practice.a: Any three: tech/software companies (1); cyber security firms (1); banks/financial companies (1); health trusts/hospitals (1); councils/civil service (1); manufacturers (1); schools/colleges (1).

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **hybrid working**.
practice.a: Splitting the working week (1) between working in the office and working from home (1).

practice.q: Explain **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of remote working for someone living in Fermanagh.
practice.a: Advantage, e.g. can work for a Belfast company without moving/long commute (1). Disadvantage, e.g. harder to learn from colleagues / needs reliable broadband / can feel isolated (1).

pages.spec: Describe the qualification route from KS3 through GCSE and A level Digital Technology (CCEA) and what each stage involves
pages.summary: At ERGS, GCSE Digital Technology follows CCEA Route B: Programming (Units 1, 4 and 5). A level Digital Technology (CCEA) builds on it with systems development, information systems and an application development project.

diagram.title: Routes into a tech career
diagram.caption: Click each stage. There is more than one way to reach the same job.

nodes.label: KS3 Digital Technology
nodes.detail: Years 8 to 10: coding, design, data, networks, online safety and AI.

blocks.text: In Year 10 you choose your GCSE subjects. It helps to know where each choice can lead. This page follows the **qualification route** in Digital Technology from KS3 to A level.
GCSE Digital Technology at ERGS
CCEA's GCSE Digital Technology has two routes. At ERGS you follow **Route B: Programming**, which leads to *GCSE Digital Technology (Programming)*. It has three units:

head: Unit
What it covers
How it is assessed
Weighting
rows: Hardware, software, networks, data, cyber security, the law and the impact of technology
Programming concepts: algorithms, data types, testing, writing and reading code
Plan, build, test and evaluate your own programmed solution
blocks.caption: CCEA GCSE Digital Technology, Route B: Programming

blocks.text: Route A (Multimedia) swaps Units 4 and 5 for Units 2 and 3, which focus on digital authoring such as websites and multimedia. Both routes include Unit 1.

A **[[Controlled assessment]]** is work completed in school under set conditions, marked by your teacher and checked (moderated) by the exam board. In Unit 5 you programme a real solution, just as a developer would.
A level Digital Technology (CCEA)

head: Unit
Assessment
Share of the A level
rows: Portfolio, marked in school and moderated by CCEA
blocks.caption: CCEA GCE Digital Technology

blocks.text: Many people who go into computing also study **maths**, a science or another subject they enjoy. Universities usually look at your whole set of A levels (or equivalent), not just one subject.
Qualification levels

Qualifications are given a **[[Qualification level]]** so you can compare them: GCSEs at grades A* to C (or 9 to 4) are level 2, A levels are level 3, a foundation degree is level 5, a bachelor's degree is level 6 and a master's degree is level 7. Apprenticeships use the same levels.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the GCSE table
blocks.context: Roisin gets 70% of the marks in Unit 4. How many percentage points of the whole GCSE has she gained from Unit 4?
steps: Unit 4 is worth **40%** of the GCSE.
So Unit 4 gives her 28 out of a possible 40 percentage points.

blocks.text: Do not think you need GCSE Digital Technology to have *any* tech career: people come in from maths, science, art and many other routes. But it gives you a big head start, especially in programming.

blocks.title: Key points
items: At ERGS, GCSE Digital Technology is CCEA Route B: Programming.
Unit 1 (exam, 30%), Unit 4 (exam, 40%), Unit 5 (controlled assessment, 30%).
A level Digital Technology has four units: AS 1, AS 2, A2 1 and A2 2.
GCSEs are level 2, A levels level 3, a bachelor's degree level 6.
There is more than one route to a tech career.

check.q: Which GCSE route do ERGS pupils follow in Digital Technology?
check.why: ERGS follows CCEA Route B: Programming (Units 1, 4 and 5).

check.q: How is GCSE Unit 5: Digital Development Practice assessed?
check.why: Unit 5 is a controlled assessment where you build a programmed solution.

check.q: Which unit is worth the most in the Route B GCSE?
check.why: Unit 4: Digital Development Concepts is worth 40%.

check.q: What qualification level is an A level?
check.why: GCSEs are level 2 and A levels are level 3.

practice.q: Name the **three** units in CCEA GCSE Digital Technology Route B.
practice.a: Unit 1 Digital Technology (1); Unit 4 Digital Development Concepts (1); Unit 5 Digital Development Practice (1).

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **controlled assessment**.
practice.a: Work completed in school under set/supervised conditions (1), marked by the teacher and moderated by the exam board (1).

practice.q: A pupil scores 50% in Unit 1. How many percentage points of the whole GCSE is this? Show your working.
practice.a: Unit 1 is worth 30% (1); 0.5 × 30 = 15 percentage points (1).

pages.spec: Compare university degrees with apprenticeships, including ApprenticeshipsNI and Higher Level Apprenticeships in Northern Ireland
pages.summary: After school you can study for a degree at university, or earn while you learn on an apprenticeship. In NI, ApprenticeshipsNI covers levels 2 and 3, and Higher Level Apprenticeships cover levels 4 to 7, up to degree and master's level.

diagram.title: University or Higher Level Apprenticeship?
diagram.caption: Both can lead to the same jobs. Which suits you better?

states.label: University degree
points: Pay tuition fees (usually with a student loan)
Lots of time to explore the subject in depth

states.label: Higher Level Apprenticeship
points: A real job with an employer, plus study
Paid a wage; no higher education tuition fees to pay
Levels 4 to 7, at least two years

blocks.text: After A levels (or sometimes after GCSEs) there are two main ways to train for a tech career: go to **university** or start an **[[Apprenticeship]]**. Neither is better: they suit different people.
University

A **degree** is a qualification from a university, usually taking three or four years full time. Popular tech degrees include computer science, software engineering, cyber security, data science and games development. Many include a **placement year** working in a company.

items: In Northern Ireland: **Queen's University Belfast**, **Ulster University** (campuses in Belfast, Coleraine and Derry~Londonderry) and the **Open University** (study online).
Many NI students also study in Great Britain or the Republic of Ireland; Atlantic Technological University has a campus in Sligo, not far from Enniskillen.
You usually pay tuition fees, normally with a student loan you repay once you earn above a set amount.

blocks.text: Apprenticeships in Northern Ireland

An apprenticeship is a **real job** with training: you work for an employer and study part of the time, usually at a further education college or university. You are paid, and you finish with a qualification **and** work experience.

head: Programme
Level
Comparable to
Who it suits
rows: People leaving school at 16 or 18 who want to start work straight away
Foundation degree up to bachelor's or master's degree
People with A levels or equivalent who want a higher qualification while earning
blocks.caption: Apprenticeship programmes run by the Department for the Economy

items: You must be at least school leaving age (16) and work at least **21 hours a week** (including training).
Apprenticeships take **at least two years**.
HLAs are available in more than 20 areas, including **ICT**, through NI's further education colleges and universities.
**South West College**, which has a campus in Enniskillen, offers Higher Level Apprenticeships in computing.

blocks.text: In England you will hear the phrase **degree apprenticeship**. In Northern Ireland, the same idea is a **Higher Level Apprenticeship at level 6** (bachelor's degree level). Names change, so always check the current nidirect apprenticeships pages.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a route
blocks.context: Aisling wants to be a software developer. She learns best by doing, wants to earn money soon, and does not want a large student loan. Kian loves theory and wants to try a placement year abroad. Suggest a route for each.
steps: Aisling: a **Higher Level Apprenticeship** in software development. She works for an employer, is paid, and does not pay higher education tuition fees.
Kian: a **university degree** in computer science with a placement year, which gives depth and time to explore.
blocks.answer: Both routes can lead to a job as a software developer; the best one depends on how you like to learn.

blocks.text: A common myth is that apprenticeships are only for people who 'could not get into university'. Higher Level Apprenticeships go up to degree and master's level, and places with top employers can be very competitive.

blocks.title: Key points
items: University degrees usually take 3 to 4 years of full-time study.
Apprenticeships combine a paid job with training.
ApprenticeshipsNI: levels 2 and 3. Higher Level Apprenticeships: levels 4 to 7.
You must be at least 16 and work at least 21 hours a week; apprenticeships take at least two years.
Both routes can lead to the same tech jobs.

check.q: What levels do Higher Level Apprenticeships in NI cover?
check.why: HLAs run from level 4 up to level 7 (master's level).

check.q: Which is TRUE of an apprenticeship?
o: You study full time and are not paid
You must already have a degree
You work for an employer, are paid and also train
check.why: An apprenticeship is a real, paid job with training built in.

check.q: What is the minimum number of hours a week an NI apprentice must work (including training)?
check.why: Apprentices must work at least 21 hours a week.

check.q: In NI, what is the equivalent of an English 'degree apprenticeship'?
o: A Higher Level Apprenticeship at level 6
check.why: Level 6 is bachelor's degree level.

practice.q: Give **two** advantages of a Higher Level Apprenticeship compared with a full-time degree.
practice.a: Any two: paid a wage (1); no higher education tuition fees (1); real work experience from the start (1); learn by doing (1).

practice.q: Give **two** advantages of going to university.
practice.a: Any two: time to study the subject in depth (1); wider choice of courses (1); placement year/study abroad (1); student life/independence (1).

practice.q: State the levels covered by ApprenticeshipsNI and by Higher Level Apprenticeships.
practice.a: ApprenticeshipsNI: levels 2 and 3 (1). HLAs: levels 4 to 7 (1).

pages.spec: Describe the skills employers look for, such as problem solving, teamwork, communication and resilience, and show evidence of them using STAR
pages.summary: Employers want technical skills, but they also want problem solving, teamwork, communication and resilience. Saying you have a skill is not enough: use the STAR method to give evidence.

diagram.title: Turn a claim into evidence
diagram.caption: Each claim is weak on its own. Click to see stronger evidence.
head: Weak claim
Skill
Stronger evidence
rows: I found and fixed a bug that made my quiz program give the wrong score.
I shared the coding with two classmates on our website project and we met every deadline.
I presented our app to Year 8 and answered their questions.
My micro:bit game failed testing three times; I kept a log and fixed each fault.
I planned my project in a timeline and finished a week early.

blocks.text: Job adverts in tech always ask for technical skills such as programming. But ask employers what they find hardest to recruit, and they often say the *other* skills: the ones that make someone good to work with. These are often called **[[Soft skills]]**.
The skills employers look for

head: Skill
What it means
How you use it in Digital Technology
rows: Breaking a problem down, trying solutions and checking they work
Decomposing a task, writing an algorithm, debugging code
Working well with others towards a shared goal
Group projects, pair programming, sharing work in an online workspace
Explaining ideas clearly to different audiences
Presenting a project, writing instructions, emailing politely
Keeping going when things go wrong and learning from mistakes
Fixing errors when code will not run, retesting after a failure
Coming up with new ideas and designs
Designing a game, a website or a logo
Planning a project in stages and keeping to them
blocks.caption: Skills employers value

blocks.text: Notice that almost all of these appear in your Digital Technology lessons. Every time you debug a program, you are practising **problem solving** and **resilience**.
Show, don't tell: the STAR method
Anyone can write *'I am a good team player'*. To convince an employer, give **evidence**. The **[[STAR method]]** helps you describe an example clearly:

items: **S**ituation: where were you and what was happening?
**T**ask: what did you need to do?
**A**ction: what did *you* do? (Say *I*, not just *we*.)
**R**esult: what happened, and what did you learn?

blocks.title: Worked example: a STAR answer for resilience
blocks.context: Write a STAR answer to the interview question 'Tell me about a time something went wrong.'
steps: **Situation:** In Year 9 our team was building a website for a local charity shop.
**Task:** I was responsible for the page that showed the opening hours and a map.
**Action:** The day before the deadline the map stopped loading. I checked my code line by line, found a missing closing tag, fixed it and tested the page on a phone and a laptop.
**Result:** The site was finished on time. I learned to test on different devices early, not at the last minute.
blocks.answer: A clear story with a real result is far more convincing than saying 'I am resilient'.

blocks.text: A common mistake is to describe what the *team* did and never what *you* did. Employers want to know your part, so use 'I' in the Action step.
Keep a simple **skills log**: each time you finish a project, write one STAR example. By Year 12 you will have plenty of evidence for applications.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Employers want technical skills and soft skills.
Key skills: problem solving, teamwork, communication, resilience, creativity, organisation.
Digital Technology lessons give you evidence of all of these.
Use STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Give real examples instead of just claiming a skill.

check.q: What does the A in STAR stand for?
check.why: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

check.q: Which is the best definition of resilience?
o: Keeping going when things go wrong and learning from it
check.why: Resilience is bouncing back from setbacks.

check.q: Which statement gives the strongest evidence of teamwork?
o: I split the coding with two classmates and we met every deadline.
check.why: A specific example with a result is real evidence.

check.q: When fixing errors in code, which two skills are you mainly practising?
check.why: Debugging means breaking the problem down and persisting until it works.

practice.q: Name **four** skills employers look for, other than programming.
practice.a: Any four: problem solving, teamwork, communication, resilience, creativity, organisation (1 each).

practice.q: What do the letters of STAR stand for?
practice.a: Situation, Task (1); Action, Result (1).

practice.q: Write a short STAR example showing problem solving from a Digital Technology lesson.
practice.a: Situation (1); Task (1); Action using 'I' and a specific step (1); Result with outcome or learning (1).

pages.spec: Explain how to build a portfolio of digital work through projects, clubs, competitions and programmes such as TechFirst
pages.summary: A portfolio is a collection of your best work that shows what you can do. Build it from school projects, your own projects, coding clubs, competitions such as Bebras and the TechFirst Girls Competition, and STEM events.

diagram.title: What does it show?
diagram.caption: Match each portfolio item to the skill it best shows an employer.
pairs: A game you made and kept improving
A website built for a local club
A team result in a cyber competition
A short video explaining your app
A data project with clear charts

blocks.text: When you apply for a course, apprenticeship or job, you will say what you can do. A **[[Portfolio]]** lets you **show** it. It is a collection of your best work, with a short explanation of each piece.
What can go in a portfolio?

items: **School projects:** your best programs, websites, databases and designs from KS3 and GCSE (keep copies!).
**Personal projects:** a game you made at home, an app to solve a problem in your family, a website for a club.
**Clubs:** a school coding club, **Code Club** or **CoderDojo** (free volunteer-led clubs supported by the Raspberry Pi Foundation).
**Competitions and challenges:** certificates and what you learned.
**Volunteering and work experience:** helping older people use tablets, running the sound desk at a school show.

blocks.text: Competitions and programmes to look out for

head: Name
What it is
rows: A UK government tech skills programme for young people. In 2026 it replaced CyberFirst; the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) leads its cyber pathway. Belfast Met is the Northern Ireland partner.
Team competition for girls (Year 9 in Northern Ireland), teams of up to four. It took over from the CyberFirst Girls Competition, which ran from 2016 to 2025.
A free computational thinking challenge held each November, run by the Raspberry Pi Foundation.
A free online platform for learning computer science, made with the University of Cambridge and the Raspberry Pi Foundation.
Legal cyber security puzzles: crack a cipher or find a hidden 'flag' in a file.
Northern Ireland's science and technology fair, where pupils show their own STEM projects.
blocks.caption: Ways to build experience while at school

blocks.text: A **[[Hackathon]]** is an event where people work in teams for a short time, often a day or a weekend, to build a solution to a challenge. Some universities and companies run hackathons for school pupils.
Presenting your portfolio

items: Choose **quality over quantity**: three to six of your best pieces.
For each piece, explain the **problem**, **who it was for**, what **you** did, and what you would **improve**.
Include screenshots or a short video, plus code if it is a programming project.
Show **progress**: an early version and an improved version tells a great story.

blocks.title: Worked example: describing a portfolio piece
blocks.context: Write a short portfolio description for a Year 10 project: a quiz app about Fermanagh history.
steps: **Problem:** Year 8 pupils found it hard to remember key dates for their local history project.
**Users:** Year 8 pupils, so I used large buttons and simple language.
**What I did:** I wrote the quiz in Python using a list of questions, and tested it with five Year 8 pupils.
**Improvement:** Testers wanted a score table, so I added one in version 2.
blocks.answer: A good description covers problem, users, your actions and how you refined it.

blocks.text: Never put other people's work, or code copied from the internet or produced by AI, in your portfolio as if you made it yourself. Always credit sources. Being caught passing off work is far worse than having a smaller portfolio.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A portfolio is a collection of your best work that proves your skills.
Include school projects, personal projects, clubs, competitions and volunteering.
TechFirst replaced CyberFirst in 2026; the TechFirst Girls Competition is for Year 9 girls in NI.
Bebras, CTFs, hackathons and Sentinus Young Innovators are great experience.
For each piece: problem, users, what you did, what you would improve.

check.q: What is a portfolio?
o: A collection of your best work that shows your skills
A list of your exam grades
check.why: A portfolio shows evidence of what you can do.

check.q: Which programme replaced CyberFirst in 2026?
check.why: CyberFirst became part of the larger TechFirst programme, with the NCSC leading the cyber pathway.

check.q: What is a hackathon?
o: An illegal attack on a website
A team event to build a solution in a short time
check.why: Hackathons are short, intense building events, usually in teams.

check.q: Which year group in NI is the TechFirst Girls Competition aimed at?
check.why: In NI it is for Year 9 girls (Year 8 in England and Wales).

practice.q: Suggest **three** things a Year 10 pupil could add to a digital portfolio.
practice.a: Any three: school project (1); personal project (1); club work (1); competition certificate/result (1); volunteering/work experience (1).

practice.q: Describe what should be included when explaining a piece of work in a portfolio.
practice.a: Any three: the problem (1); who it was for/users (1); what you did (1); how you tested/refined it or what you would improve (1).

practice.q: Explain why you should never present AI-generated or copied code as your own work.
practice.a: It is dishonest/plagiarism/breaks copyright (1) and could lose you a place or job if discovered / does not show your real skills (1).

pages.spec: Explain how your digital footprint and online reputation can affect your future, and how to behave professionally online
pages.summary: Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave online, and it shapes your online reputation. Universities and employers may look you up, so think before you post and use online spaces professionally.

diagram.title: Before you post: the think-first check
diagram.caption: Follow the questions. If any answer is a problem, do not post.

nodes.label: I want to post something
nodes.detail: A photo, comment, video or message.

nodes.label: Would I be happy for a future employer to see it?
nodes.detail: Imagine it on a big screen at a job interview.

nodes.label: Is it kind, true and fair to others?
nodes.detail: Does it embarrass, upset or mislead anyone? Do I have permission for photos of others?

nodes.label: Does it share private information?
nodes.detail: Address, school, passwords, location, other people's details.

nodes.label: Do not post it
nodes.detail: Change it, keep it private or leave it. Deleted posts can still have been copied.

nodes.label: OK to post
nodes.detail: Still check your privacy settings and who can see it.

blocks.text: Everything you do online leaves a trace: posts, likes, comments, photos you are tagged in, game usernames and more. This is your **[[Digital footprint]]**.

Your **[[Online reputation]]** is what people think of you based on what they can find. When you apply for a part-time job, a course or an apprenticeship, the person deciding may search for your name.
Why it matters for your career

items: Posts can be **screenshotted and shared**, so 'deleted' does not mean gone.
Something you post at 14 could still be found when you are 18 and applying for jobs.
Offensive jokes, bullying or posts about illegal behaviour can cost people places and jobs.
A **positive** footprint helps: a project you shared, a club you helped run or a competition you entered.

blocks.text: Professionalism online
**[[Professionalism]]** means behaving in a way that is reliable, respectful and appropriate for work or study. Online that means:

head: Unprofessional
Professional
rows: Email address based on your name, e.g. **aoife.byrne@...**
Message to a teacher: *'hey wheres the homework'*
*'Hello Mr Butler, could you tell me where this week's homework is? Thank you, Aoife.'*
Disagreeing politely, or not replying at all
Public profile with location and school shown
Privacy settings checked; personal details kept private
Using someone else's work without credit
blocks.caption: Online behaviour that helps or harms your reputation

blocks.title: Worked example: what would an employer think?
blocks.context: Eoin applies for a Saturday job in an Enniskillen computer shop. The manager searches his name and finds (a) a gaming video where he swears at other players, and (b) a website he built for his local GAA club. What impression does each give?
steps: (a) Shows poor self-control and disrespect: a **negative** impression for a customer-facing job.
(b) Shows real web skills, community involvement and reliability: a **positive** impression.
Eoin should make the video private or delete it, check what else is public, and mention the GAA website in his application.
blocks.answer: The same search can help or harm you; you control much of what people find.

blocks.text: Privacy settings help, but they are not a guarantee. Friends can share your posts, and companies can change their settings. The safest rule: if you would not want a future employer to see it, do not post it.

Search your own name (with a parent or carer) once in a while to see what others can find. Also check the minimum age in a site's terms before you join it: most social media sites require users to be at least 13.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave online.
Your online reputation is what people think of you from what they find.
Posts can be copied, so deleted is not always gone.
Use a sensible email address and polite, clear messages.
Build a positive footprint by sharing work you are proud of.

check.q: What is a digital footprint?
o: The trail of data you leave online
A fingerprint scanner on a phone
check.why: Posts, likes, comments and tags all add to your digital footprint.

check.q: Which email address is most professional for a job application?
check.why: An address based on your name looks professional.

check.q: Why is 'I deleted it' not always enough?
o: Deleted posts always come back after a week
Others may already have screenshotted or shared it
check.why: Once posted, content can be copied and shared.

check.q: Which of these would build a POSITIVE online reputation?
o: Sharing a friend's photo without asking
Sharing a website you built for a local club
check.why: Showing your work and community involvement creates a positive footprint.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **digital footprint** and an **online reputation**.
practice.a: Digital footprint: the trail of data/content you leave online (1). Online reputation: what people think of you based on that content (1).

practice.q: Give **two** ways a pupil could improve their online reputation before applying for a job.
practice.a: Any two: delete/hide unsuitable posts (1); check privacy settings (1); use a professional email (1); share positive work/projects (1).

practice.q: Rewrite this message so it is professional: 'hey cant come 2 work tmrw im sick'.
practice.a: Polite greeting and sign-off with name (1); clear, correctly spelt message, e.g. 'Hello Mrs Kelly, I'm sorry but I am unwell and won't be able to work tomorrow. ...' (1).

pages.spec: Write a skills-based CV and plan a personal statement for a tech course or job
pages.summary: A skills-based CV puts your skills and evidence first, which suits young people with little work experience. A personal statement explains why you want a course and how you have prepared; UCAS now asks three questions in 4,000 characters.

diagram.title: Personal statement character counter
diagram.caption: UCAS gives you 4,000 characters in total across three answers. Change the lengths to see how many characters you have left.

inputs.label: Answer 2: how your studies prepared you
Answer 3: what else you have done

blocks.text: A **[[CV]]** (curriculum vitae) is a short document, usually no more than two pages, that summarises your skills, education and experience for an employer. You will need one for part-time jobs, work experience and apprenticeships.
What is a skills-based CV?

A traditional CV lists jobs you have had. At 15 or 16 you probably have not had many! A **[[Skills-based CV]]** puts your **skills first**, each backed by evidence from school, clubs, hobbies or volunteering.

head: Section
What to include
rows: Name, phone number and a professional email address. Your town is enough: you do not need your full address.
Two or three sentences: who you are, what you are good at and what you are looking for.
Three to five skills, each with a short example as evidence (use STAR ideas).
Your school and the GCSE subjects you are taking or have taken.
Part-time jobs, work experience, volunteering, helping run a club.
Competitions, awards, projects, sports, music: things that show something about you.
Say *'References available on request'*, and ask a teacher's permission before naming them.
blocks.caption: Sections of a skills-based CV

blocks.title: Worked example: improving a 'Key skills' entry
blocks.context: Sinéad's CV says: 'IT skills: good with computers.' Improve it.
steps: The original is vague: *every* applicant could say it.
Name specific skills: programming in Python, spreadsheets, web design.
Add evidence: *'Built a spreadsheet to track sales for our school tuck shop, using formulas and charts to show the best-selling items.'*
blocks.answer: 'Digital skills: Python programming and spreadsheets. Built a tuck shop spreadsheet with formulas and charts that helped choose which snacks to stock.'

blocks.text: Check spelling and grammar carefully. Spelling mistakes on a CV suggest you are careless, which is especially bad for a job that needs attention to detail, such as testing software. And never lie on a CV.
Personal statements

A **[[Personal statement]]** is a piece of writing where you explain why you want a course or job and why you would be good at it. You will write one for university applications (through **UCAS**) and often for apprenticeships.
For courses starting from 2026, UCAS replaced the single long essay with **three questions**, answered in **4,000 characters in total**:

items: Why do you want to study this course or subject?
How have your qualifications and studies helped you to prepare for this course or subject?
What else have you done to prepare outside of education, and why are these experiences useful?

blocks.text: For a tech course, strong answers mention real projects, what you learned from your GCSE and A level coursework, competitions, clubs, reading about technology and work experience. Specific beats general every time.
Start a *'useful for my CV'* note now. Write down projects, competitions, roles and achievements as they happen. In Year 13 you will be glad you did.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A CV summarises your skills, education and experience, usually in two pages or fewer.
A skills-based CV puts skills and evidence first: ideal when you have little work experience.
Use a professional email, check spelling and never lie.
A personal statement explains why you want a course and how you have prepared.
UCAS now asks three questions, 4,000 characters in total.

check.q: What does a skills-based CV put first?
o: A list of every job you have had
check.why: Skills-based CVs focus on what you can do, which suits young people.

check.q: How many characters does UCAS allow in total for the personal statement?
check.why: 4,000 characters across the three questions.

check.q: Which is the best 'Key skills' entry?
o: Python: wrote a quiz program and tested it with Year 8 pupils.
check.why: It names a skill and gives specific evidence.

check.q: Before naming a teacher as a referee you should...
check.why: Always ask before naming someone as a referee.

practice.q: List **four** sections you would include in a skills-based CV.
practice.a: Any four: contact details, personal profile, key skills, education, experience, achievements/interests, references (1 each).

practice.q: Explain why a skills-based CV suits a Year 11 pupil better than a traditional CV.
practice.a: They have little or no work history (1), so putting skills with evidence from school/clubs/hobbies first shows what they can do (1).

practice.q: Write a two-sentence personal profile for a CV for a Saturday job in a computer shop.
practice.a: Who you are and key strengths (1); what you are looking for / why this job (1).

pages.spec: Explain why diversity matters in technology and challenge myths and stereotypes about who 'does' computing
pages.summary: Women and other groups are under-represented in tech: in 2025 only about 22% of UK IT specialists were women. Diverse teams build better, fairer products, and the stereotype of who 'does' computing is simply wrong.

diagram.title: Myth or reality?
diagram.caption: Common myths about who works in computing, and what is actually true.

states.label: Myths
points: You must be a maths genius
Tech people work alone and never talk
You need to have coded since you were six

states.label: Reality
points: Women have shaped computing from the very start
Problem solving and practice matter more than genius
Tech is teamwork: lots of talking, planning and explaining
Many people start coding at school, college or later

blocks.text: A **[[Stereotype]]** is a fixed, over-simple idea about what a group of people is like. The stereotype of a programmer is a young man alone in a dark room. It puts many people off before they have even tried, and it is not true.
The numbers

According to BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT, about **22%** of IT specialists in the UK workforce in **2025** were women. That means roughly **one in five**. Women make up about half the population, so they are clearly **under-represented**.

blocks.title: Worked example: what does 22% mean?
blocks.context: A Belfast tech company has 150 IT specialists. If it matched the UK figure of 22% women, how many would be women? How many would there be at 50%?
steps: The difference is 75 − 33 = **42** people.
blocks.answer: 33 at 22%, compared with 75 if the team matched the population.

blocks.text: Women who shaped computing

head: Person
What she did
rows: Wrote notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, including what is often called the first published computer program.
US Navy computer scientist who helped develop early compilers and the COBOL language. She helped popularise the word *debugging*.
NASA mathematician whose calculations helped send astronauts into orbit and to the Moon.
Led the team that wrote the on-board flight software for the Apollo Moon missions.
British computer scientist whose ideas about weighting words are still used by search engines.
blocks.caption: Some women who changed computing

blocks.text: Why diversity matters
**[[Diversity]]** means including people of different genders, backgrounds, ethnicities, ages, abilities and ways of thinking. In tech this is not just about fairness: it makes products better.

items: A team that all thinks alike can miss problems that affect other users.
AI trained on data from only one group of people can work badly, or unfairly, for everyone else.
A team that includes disabled people is more likely to build **accessible** products.
Different ideas lead to more creative solutions.

blocks.text: Do not let a stereotype decide your GCSE choices for you. If you enjoy solving problems, making things or helping people, there is a place for you in tech, whoever you are.
Programmes such as the **TechFirst Girls Competition** exist to encourage girls to try computing early, and many NI tech companies run events aimed at girls and under-represented groups.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A stereotype is a fixed, over-simple idea about a group.
In 2025 about 22% of UK IT specialists were women.
Women such as Ada Lovelace, Grace Hopper and Margaret Hamilton shaped computing.
Diverse teams build fairer, more accessible and more creative products.
You do not need to be a genius or start at six: practice matters most.

check.q: About what percentage of UK IT specialists were women in 2025?
check.why: BCS reported about 22%, roughly one in five.

check.q: Who wrote what is often called the first published computer program?
check.why: Ada Lovelace wrote it for Babbage's Analytical Engine in the 1840s.

check.q: Why can a lack of diversity make AI systems worse?
o: AI needs a person of every age to switch it on
AI trained on data from one group can work badly for others
check.why: Biased data can lead to biased results.

check.q: Which statement is a myth?
o: Tech work involves lots of teamwork
You must be a maths genius to work in tech
Many people learn to code at school or later
Women have shaped computing from the start
check.why: Problem solving and practice matter more than genius.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by a **stereotype**, using an example from computing.
practice.a: A fixed, over-simple idea about what a group is like (1), e.g. that programmers are all boys who work alone (1).

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why diverse tech teams can build better products.
practice.a: Any two: spot problems affecting different users (1); fairer AI/less biased data (1); more accessible products (1); more creative ideas (1).

practice.q: Name **one** woman who made an important contribution to computing and describe what she did.
practice.a: Name (1) and correct contribution (1), e.g. Margaret Hamilton led the Apollo flight software team.

pages.spec: Create a personal careers plan with SMART targets for your next steps
pages.summary: A careers plan sets out where you might like to go and the steps to get there. Use SMART targets, gain work experience, talk to the Careers Service and review your plan as your interests change.

diagram.title: Example careers plan: Caoimhe, Year 10
diagram.caption: One pupil's plan from Year 10 to Year 14. Click each stage to see her targets.

items.label: Year 10: explore
items.detail: Choose GCSEs including Digital Technology and maths. Join the school coding club. Enter Bebras in November.

items.label: Year 11: build
items.detail: Make a personal website to hold her portfolio. Volunteer to help at the school open night tech stand.

items.label: Year 12: test it out
items.detail: Work experience in an IT department. Meet a Careers Service adviser. Finish her Unit 5 controlled assessment project.

items.label: Years 13 and 14: decide
items.detail: A level Digital Technology. Compare university courses with Higher Level Apprenticeships; apply to both.

items.label: After school
items.detail: A software development HLA or a computing degree. Review the plan every year.

blocks.text: You do not need to know your exact future job in Year 10. Most adults change jobs several times, and some of the jobs you will do have not been invented yet. But a **[[Careers plan]]** helps you make good choices now and keeps your options open.
Step 1: know yourself

items: What do I **enjoy**? (Making things, solving puzzles, helping people, design, data...)
What am I **good at**? (Look at reports, feedback and projects.)
What **matters** to me? (Working with people, being creative, helping the environment, earning well, staying in Fermanagh...)

blocks.text: Step 2: explore options

items: Research the six career areas on pages 2 and 3, and look at real job adverts to see what they ask for.
Talk to your careers teacher and a **Careers Service** adviser.
Ask family and friends who work with technology what their job is really like.
Look at college, university and apprenticeship course pages to see entry requirements.

blocks.text: Step 3: set SMART targets

A **[[SMART target]]** is a goal that is **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**elevant and **T**ime-bound. *'Get better at coding'* is not SMART. *'Finish the first ten Python challenges on our class site by the Easter holidays'* is.

head: Weak target
SMART target
rows: Join the school coding club and attend every week until June.
Email three local businesses by 1 March asking about a week of work experience in Year 12.
Put my three best KS3 projects, with descriptions, into a portfolio by the end of Year 10.
Get at least 70% in each GCSE Unit 4 practice paper by the end of Year 11.
blocks.caption: Making targets SMART

blocks.text: Step 4: get experience

**[[Work experience]]** means spending time in a real workplace to see what a job is like. Schools often arrange it in Year 12 or Year 13, but you can also gain experience through part-time jobs, volunteering, open days and online taster events.

blocks.title: Worked example: is it SMART?
blocks.context: Decide whether each target is SMART and fix it if not. (a) 'Learn about cyber security.' (b) 'Enter the TechFirst Girls Competition with my friends this November and complete every challenge.'
steps: (a) Not SMART: not specific, not measurable and no deadline. Better: *'Complete three beginner cipher challenges and write up what I learned in my portfolio by the end of term.'*
(b) SMART: specific (one named competition), measurable (every challenge), achievable, relevant to a cyber interest, and time-bound (this November).

blocks.text: A careers plan is not a contract. If you discover you love UX design instead of networking, change the plan! Review it at least once a year, for example when you get your report.
Keep your options open by choosing GCSEs you enjoy and are good at. Digital Technology combined with subjects such as maths, a science, art or English keeps many tech routes available.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A careers plan helps you make good choices now and keeps options open.
Know yourself, explore options, set SMART targets, get experience.
SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
Work experience shows you what a job is really like.
Review and change your plan as your interests change.

check.q: What does the T in SMART stand for?
check.why: SMART targets have a deadline.

check.q: Which target is SMART?
o: Join the coding club and attend every week until June
check.why: It is specific, measurable and has a time limit.

check.q: What is work experience?
o: Time spent in a real workplace to see what a job is like
A job you are paid a full salary for
check.why: Work experience lets you try a job before you choose it.

o: Never: it is fixed once written
At least once a year, and whenever your interests change
Only if a teacher forces you

practice.q: What does SMART stand for?
practice.a: Specific, Measurable (1); Achievable, Relevant (1); Time-bound (1).

practice.q: Rewrite 'get some work experience' as a SMART target.
practice.a: Specific action (e.g. email three named businesses) (1) with a deadline / measurable outcome (1).

practice.q: Give **two** ways a Year 10 pupil could find out more about careers in digital technology.
practice.a: Any two: Careers Service adviser/careers teacher (1); research job adverts/course pages (1); ask people who work in tech (1); clubs/competitions/open days (1).

glossary.def: The abilities needed to use, understand and create with digital technology, from using software confidently to writing code.
A skill that can be used in many different jobs or subjects, such as problem solving or communication.
Using computers and machines to do tasks automatically that people used to do by hand.
A person who designs, writes, tests and improves computer programs. Also called a programmer or software engineer.
A person who watches an organisation's systems for signs of attack and responds when something goes wrong.
A person who collects, cleans and analyses data to find patterns, and often builds AI models that make predictions.
A person who designs, builds and maintains the networks that connect computers.
Storing data and running software on servers in data centres, reached over the internet, instead of on your own device.
A user experience designer: someone who researches users' needs and designs products that are easy and accessible to use.
A person who plans the rules, levels, characters and story of a game, and tests that it is fun.
A person who sets up, maintains and fixes technology and helps users with problems. Often a first job in tech.
All the businesses whose main product is software, digital services or technology.
Splitting the working week between the workplace and home.
Working from home, or anywhere away from the office, for all or nearly all of the time.
Coursework completed in school under set conditions, marked by the teacher and moderated by the exam board.
A number used to compare qualifications: GCSEs are level 2, A levels level 3, a bachelor's degree level 6.
A paid job that includes training towards a recognised qualification.
An NI apprenticeship at levels 4 to 7, from foundation degree up to master's level, combining paid work with study.
Personal skills that help you work well with others, such as communication, teamwork and resilience.
The ability to keep going when things go wrong and to learn from mistakes.
A way of giving evidence of a skill: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
A collection of your best work, with explanations, that shows what you can do.
A legal cyber security competition where players solve puzzles to find hidden 'flags'.
An event where people work in teams for a short time to build a solution to a challenge.
The trail of data you leave online, such as posts, likes, comments and photos.
What other people think of you based on what they can find about you online.
Behaving in a reliable, respectful and appropriate way for work or study.
Curriculum vitae: a short document summarising your skills, education and experience for an employer.
A CV that puts your skills first, each backed by evidence, instead of a list of past jobs.
Writing that explains why you want a course or job and why you would be good at it.
A fixed, over-simple idea about what a group of people is like.
Including people of different genders, backgrounds, ethnicities, ages, abilities and ways of thinking.
A plan setting out your possible career goals and the steps you will take towards them.
A goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
Time spent in a real workplace to find out what a job is like.
